utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. No preliminaries were announced to us. Mr. Shin, I do understand that you have one hour and 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President, and hopefully I'll be shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrba. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Shin will now continue his cross-examination, and the Chamber is confident that we'll conclude your testimony this morning. Mr. Shin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we left off looking at some VRS documents. I'd like to show you two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 30646 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, as this document is coming up, I'll explain what it is. It's a document from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Command - now you can see it there - dated the 1st of April, 1994. And that's in the upper left-hand corner. Now just -- just below, we see that this is about conclusions and tasks from a briefing at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Command on the previous day, 31st of March, 1994. And turning briefly to the end of the document, that's the third page in English and the second page in B/C/S, we can see that it's signed by General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please turn back one page in each, so page 2 in English and page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I'd like to just direct your attention to item number 8 and I'll read it: "Fortify positions around Sarajevo by erecting wire and concrete barriers, which would, in turn, strengthen the belief that they are really blocked ('in a camp')." Now we'll go to one more document and then I'll put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we please have P327.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Skrba, while we're waiting for that document to come up I'll explain what that is. This is an intercept from the 25th of May, 1992, between General Mladic and another individual. Now if we could turn to page, English page 2 and B/C/S 2, and I'll let you find that -- I'll give you a chance to find that on the page. Yes, it's near the bottom third. And -- in B/C/S and I'll read the relevant passage: "We have the means and the bridges with which to cross the river. I have blocked Sarajevo from four corners. The city is trapped, there is no way out." Now, Mr. Skrba, we've seen the first document, from General Galic in 1994. Yesterday, we saw two documents from August 1992 referring to the VRS's blockade of Sarajevo. And now we see General Mladic making it clear from the very early days of this -- of this war, that the VRS had Sarajevo trapped, as he put it. Now, there are other documents, but let me just ask you: Do you continue to assert that these assessments of General Mladic, Colonel Sipcic, General Galic, that the VRS had blockaded Sarajevo, that these are all simply incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to say two things here. I saw the corps order and I saw the other thing. I would like to confirm what I said yesterday. I still maintain and I still believe that the BiH Army and the Presidency, if they had been blockaded, they were blockaded militarily, whereas the civilian life went on normally throughout the war. People could leave across the runway and later on the tunnel was dug out, and if they so wished, they could both enter and leave. The blockade, in my view, was a military blockade to prevent the units from leaving, and as far as the civilian population in -- is concerned, no order concerned them. I even know when the bridge on Grbavica was opened, and that was in our zone of responsibility, we allowed the civilians to cross from both sides, and the enemy side always restricted that passage. There was a window of opportunity of a couple of hours but then they had to return the following evening, and that went on for a year, in 1994 and 1994 [as interpreted]. I don't know the dates, but I know that such things happened on that bridge. In other words, the civilian population and those who needed assistance were never forbidden, not for a single moment, to leave freely. And also, as you know, those who were seriously wounded could not be operated on. They were allowed to leave and to be treated outside of Sarajevo. Those who needed assistance, humanitarian assistance, they were assisted, as far as I know. And as for the last transcript you showed me, General Mladic and those things, as you said it yourself that was on the 25th of May, and in my zone of responsibility I assumed my responsibilities from the JNA on the 27th. I was not in command position at that time, and also, I never attended any briefings at the corps command. Therefore, I don't know what was going on. I can only testify based on what you say, because I never attended any briefings. I was never invited to any briefings because my position and my duties were within the framework of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Skrba, your testimony to this Court is that civilian life continued on normally as before the war.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I didn't say that the -- that life was normal. However, what I said was that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina could cross the territory in control of the Army of Republika Srpska. They could leave freely and they could go in a desired direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm going to move onto a different topic now, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But, first, as Ms. Stewart has correctly reminded me, can we please tender 65 ter 30646.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30646 receives number P6523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, in your testimony in the Karadzic case, you were asked about the neighbourhood of Bjelave and this is what you said when the Prosecutor asked you: "Can you describe the general nature of this area, please." You said: "This is a civilian area almost 100 per cent. I think the buildings are mostly residential buildings but some are perhaps also collectively owned buildings." Do you stand by your testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday, during questions from Defence counsel, that in the area of Bjelave, the ABiH had 120-millimetre mobile mortars mounted on a vehicle, and you tried to neutralize that fire. So you fired into that area Bjelave, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We fired on the position where that 120-millimetre mortar was, and it was regular military target because, from there, it opened fire on our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you had said it was a mobile mortar. Now, what did you use to fire at it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 120-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you fired 120-millimetre mortar into Bjelave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that that was an anti-personnel weapon.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is also used to destroy small artillery weapons in order to prevent it from firing at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you accepted the risk of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as that mortar was firing from there, I had to respond. I had to neutralize it so it would stop firing on our positions and on our lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement - and Your Honours that's paragraph 24 - there's a section that's headed: "Incident G6." And it begins: "The incident of 22 January 1994 in Alipasino Polje was explained to me. It was also explained to me that the Defence team claimed that the incoming trajectory of the alleged 120-millimetre mortar shell had been south-west and that the most probable place of firing was a facility which I recognised as the Butmir agricultural estate." So clearly it was the Defence team that gave you this explanation for the origin of fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the origin of fire. They just showed me a transcript to demonstrate that there was an incident in Alipasino Polje and what happened there, and then I said that if it was in the south-west, then, from that sector, from the firing positions, in the territory held by the Muslim forces, that would have been Butmir. And I know that very well because even before the war, we went there and we carried out mobilisation efforts and we prepared the troops of the former JNA and that's why I knew that the firing positions of 120-millimetre mortars were originally planned to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, let me just go back to something you just said. You were shown a transcript. What transcript were you shown?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that I provided last time and when I testified in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in that statement as well, you explained that it was explained to you by the Defence team; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Defence team asked me about that. And then from my point of view, from my professional point of view, I showed them where approximately those positions could have been and where fire could have been opened from. Because that territory was held by the enemy forces throughout the war; the BiH Army, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a few questions. First of all, do you have any personal knowledge about this incident? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second: Have you any information available to you that would explain the distance from which the shell you were told about was fired? You say in your statement that it was explained to that you it was fired from a southwesterly direction. Did you -- do you have any reliable information as to distance? I mean, 500 metres, 3 kilometres, 6 kilometres? Do you have any reliable information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with the area because I grew up there. That's why I am familiar with the distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the distance from which the shell was fired, I'm talking about, not the distance between the place of impact and Butmir or any other. But do you have any reliable information about that shell and from what distance it was fired, apart from what direction it was fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I wasn't there. It was in the enemy territory. Alipasino Polje is where the shell fell. I didn't carry out an on-site investigation. Experts went there in order to ascertain the angle and the distance. I wasn't among them. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not inspect those records. They were never available to me. And I was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, whether the distance was such that it would or could have been fired from Butmir, you have no knowledge about that either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it was fired and from what distance, but I assume if they say south-west, I assume that it was approximately from that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next subject, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, you also address in your statement an incident G7 and again this part of your statement begins: "It was explained to me that on 4th February 1994 there was an alleged incident at Dobrinja." Now, who was it that explained this to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it in the papers. They themselves explained it, and they made it known in the media, and I learned about this incident here, at the Tribunal. At my location, Lima 5, there was a permanent team and if such incidents happened those teams and their bosses came to me and they investigated and they --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I'm sorry to interrupt. My question to you was: You said, "It was explained to me ..." Now, is your answer about who explained that to you that you meant you read it in the newspaper? Is that what that phrase means: "It was explained to me"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified in the Karadzic case, they asked me whether I was aware of that incident, and that was when I learnt about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That appears in your Karadzic statement as well. But I'll move on. For incident G --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, a while ago you said, "I read it in the papers." That is not papers published at the time of your Karadzic testimony, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was before. Those papers were published after the Dayton Accords. Every such incident that happened, Mr. President, they wrote about it in the papers, they showed it on TV, usually on the anniversary of the events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then read again one of your last answers. "When I testified in the Karadzic case, they asked me whether I was aware of that incident, and that was when I learnt about that incident." So on the one hand, you say, "I read it in the newspapers"; on another moment you say, "I learned it during my testimony in Karadzic," which is not fully consistent. Any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I testified in the Karadzic I learned about that incident. In the meantime, every year they mark the anniversaries of those incidents. They obviously have programmes on TV to remind everybody of what happened, that -- and I'm talking about the television and newspapers of the BiH Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, you just said right now that you learned of this when you testified in the Karadzic case. But isn't it a fact that actually that was in your statement presented to the Karadzic Court so, therefore, it was a matter addressed before your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In preparations for the testimony in the Karadzic case, before I came to testify, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Skrba, for this incident that you refer to as G18, in your statement this part also begins: "It was explained to me ..." Now, again I'm asking you, was it the Defence team who explained that to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was Mr. Karadzic, when I talked to him in preparations for my testimony in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions -- I'm sorry, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do have perhaps one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, could you please tell this Court what exactly it was that Mr. Karadzic said to you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me -- or, rather, he read out to me what the Prosecutor asked him, about the incidents, and I said that I didn't know about those incidents, but I -- we talked about where the shell could have come from and I told him where fire could have been opened from, approximately. And then the following year, they actually marked the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But, once again, you did not personally have any knowledge of these incidents, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. Mr. Stojanovic, any need to reexamine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of questions, Mr. Skrba. I'll start with the last things first, i.e., I'm going to ask you about incidents G6 and G7. From the positions where you were and where your units were -- where your unit was deployed, I'm talking about the MAD, could you observe the positions of the BiH Army in Butmir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the way up to Hrasnica. When they opened fire you could see detonations from their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And throughout the war, and I'm particularly interested in 1994, did you observe that fire was opened on the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska from Butmir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could see that from our observation posts which were about 5- to 600 metres high. You did not need an optical instrument, you could see it with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness be alerted to the fact that they speak the same language and that they should make a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pause between question and answer and answer and question. Mr. Stojanovic, let's -- let's resume from where the witness said that he did not need instruments but that he could see it with the naked eye. Could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The question was: And from that position, from the agricultural institute at Butmir, did the BiH Army open fire on the positions of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the agricultural institute in Butmir, and, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the situation calmed down after the war, did you ever go to that position personally?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally went by on two occasions. I was curious I'm resident of Ilidza, and in that location and in some other locations, we saw some ammunition crates, some leftovers from the war activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now we'll finish with the following question. As you are looking towards Alipasino Polje, where was the artillery of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Butmir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the south, south-west direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me. I don't understand the question. As you are looking towards Alipasino Polje, where was the artillery of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are you able to determine the direction by looking at the direction; or are you saying when he's positioned at that place at Alipasino Polje? It depends which way I'm facing when I'm looking and I'm not quite sure I understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I am standing at Alipasino Polje, to which side from the viewpoint of Alipasino Polje would be the agricultural complex of Butmir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the west, south-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And since you are a native of that area, would you tell me what is the distance, as the crow flies, from the broader area of Alipasino Polje to the agricultural complex in Butmir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies? 2 or 2 and a half kilometres. And those were the ideal positions for mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up in e-court P4435, page 2. Or, rather, let us look at the first page to see what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue there, I'm waiting for the -- waiting for that to appear on our screens, if I read your statement well, Mr. Skrba, you first imagined what would be the probable place of firing, and I'm talking about this incident in Alipasino Polje, whereas you had no information whatsoever about from what distance that shell was fired. And then you say: "According to my information, this area is ideal as firing space for mortars of all calibres." But there's no basis whatsoever to assume that that shell was fired from Butmir, was there? Apart from that it is in the direction from the impact it's -- it's all speculation, pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood me perfectly well. I just supposed, since it was from west/south-west, that it was there. Because we used to be one army, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, and before, when we had military drills, we came there together for training, and I know that from before the war, from military drills. I had colleagues, Croats and Muslims, who were there in those positions during military exercises before the war, when we had war games. That's -- that's how I made this assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did your army have positions, mortar positions, in the area of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't go there during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you went there. I asked you whether your army had positions there. If you say, "I don't know," fine, then you don't know. If you do know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know their positions or whether they had positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking about your positions, VRS. In the Nedzarici area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said. Those were positions of the battalion which was part of the Ilidza Brigade, and they had their own commander. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I -- what strikes me is that you have no problem in speculating to what happened on the other side, whereas, when I ask you about your own positions nearby, you do not speculate. You say, "I don't know, I didn't go there." You understand what I'm telling you, that you're expounding quite a bit on how well it could have been fired from the opposite without any factual knowledge, whereas, as far as your own positions, you say, "I don't know." I just wanted to put to that you to give you an opportunity to explain this if there's any explanation you'd like to give.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally I know about my unit within the Sarajevo Brigade, and that's my primary concern. As for our units and other brigades, they had a different deployment and different formations. During the war I had no time to tour the neighbouring positions of the VRS to see how they deployed, where they positioned mortars or howitzers. That's why I wasn't really knowledgeable about the positions of our army around me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently you missed the point I wanted to make, and, therefore, we leave it to that at this moment. Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions in relation to the document which is now on our screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even begin on this topic, on this document, but let us look at the next page, the passage used by the Prosecution in the cross-examination, and then I will have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, if you remember, you were asked yesterday about this paragraph, command and control. I have just a couple of questions. Until what time were you effectively a mobilised person in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 26 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tadija Manojlovic, who signed this document, if you remember, was he an active-duty officer of the then-JNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a retired colonel. A professional officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now please look at this paragraph. I'll ask you a question in this context. In his report, in his analysis, he says: "The ARJ - artillery rockets unit's command and control - may be divided into two periods: The first from the beginning of the war until 20th May 1992, and the second one from that date until today. During the first period - that means until 20th May 1992 - we managed to withdraw all the equipment, vehicles and ammunition from the barracks in a timely manner and have them positioned around Sarajevo. The MAD of the Sarajevo Mechanized Brigade, which was a component part of the then-4th Corps, had in their ranks the largest number of active-duty officers and soldiers." Now I'm asking you: This reference to active-duty officers and soldiers, is this a reference to the period until the 20th May 1992, when the JNA still existed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that within your MAD in the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, there was not a single active-duty officer. Do you mean that was the case from the establishment of the brigade, from the 20th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I meant. After they left the barracks, all the officers who were not natives of Republika Srpska left Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I had only one superior, Simic. Otherwise, in my brigade, there were no NCOs or officers. They were just local people from the environs of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrba, for this explanation. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, has this triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No, it has not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we excuse the witness, there's one issue that came to the mind of the Judges, which is the following. An important part of the testimony of this witness is that a firing position was close to an observation post and that they always explained to the observers what they were doing, that they were only firing in response. Now, the Chamber wonders whether not the testimony of this witness would have been strengthened by producing those observers' reports who would say: They came to us today and asked whether they could fire in that direction a response of, or they told us that there was -- they were fired at and they responded to that fire. I mean, those reports could either strongly support or not support, we do not know, the testimony of this witness, and the Chamber wondered whether the parties could find reports. I think the witness talked about Lima 5. So is there any reporting? Can it be produced so that the Chamber would be better able to assess the reliability of the evidence the witness has given? I'm just looking at the parties at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly do look to see anything that might contradict the witness and that might be relevant to the witness's testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not only contradict --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you see -- the Chamber is not seeking material that would contradict what the witness said but which --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, I misspoke, Your Honour. I meant relevant to it. Given the Chamber's inquiry, we'll make a specific investigation into this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Our investigation followed that direction because that corroborates the testimony of today's witness in paragraph 8. And I am sure that through our further work and with future witnesses, we will add to this evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be able to report, well, let's say, within the next month on this issue, or the next six weeks before the summer recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to this particular witness and his evidence, we will give you a report next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the recess, I think we will have done -- sorry, by the adjournment, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what adjournment you're talking about at this very moment, but ... I mean, the witness will be excused today, so whether the material which could be submitted to the Chamber, whether that would have any consequences, of course, is a matter still to be considered, once you have seen it, once we may have seen it. Then, Mr. Skrba, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions, whether these were questions put to you by the parties or questions put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again, and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And we can assist you. There are teams that stayed with us, I didn't want to mention it, but I will help the Defence team get in contact with the observers who had spent time with us, and maybe they can take their statements too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- it's appreciated that you want to assist, at least one party in these proceedings, but I think there are -- there may be reports already in existence. But don't take any action in that respect and leave it to the parties, as the Chamber does at this moment as well. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a bit shorter than we anticipated, and our witness will be here at half past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we take an early break. Yes, and we would then resume at 20 minutes to 11.00, so the witness would have been here for ten minutes by then. We take a break and resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence is ready to call its next witness now he has arrived, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are ready, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be Branko Radan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Radan. Mr. Radan, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just noticed that Mr. Radan has a -- some documents in front of him and if the Prosecution wants to examine those documents -- it's the statement and the documents probably we worked with. So if the Prosecution wants to inspect if there's anything written on the documents, they are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could take just a brief look, that would be appreciated. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, with the assistance of the usher, give whatever is before you for inspection. And I would like to ask you not to consult any documents without having informed the Chamber that you wish to do so and without having received approval to do it, and we would then ask you, most likely, what the document is you would like to consult. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I understand the layout of the documents. My only question is that within the documents there appears to be an original handwritten note. I would simply -- I can't read it. But I would simply inquire as to the contents of the note. That seems to be the only thing that -- that doesn't fit within the categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if the witness would not consult any of the documents, then, of course, it's not very relevant to know what is in the handwritten note.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could simply be provided with a copy of the handwritten note at some point today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, all I need with the witness to stay is his statement, so everything else can be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If then a clean copy of the statement could be provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's clean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clean. But, then, Mr. Lukic, could you please, with the assistance of the usher, then select what exactly -- because I see it is a bit of a bundle. Could you please select what you consider and all the rest then should be -- if you would show what the witness has selected, Mr. Usher, to Mr. Lukic, if that's the -- exclusively the statement, then we are there. Mr. Lukic, all the rest, perhaps you later return it to the witness because it's his property. I don't know whether he wants you to read his handwritten notes or not. So you -- all the rest is with Mr. Lukic. You'll get it back - I would say, when we have the first break, it can be returned to the witness - and you have now a copy of your statement available to you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We did not have time to meet up earlier today. I was busy in the Defence room, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull up 1D1608 on the screen. It's Mr. Radan's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see page 1 of this document on the screen. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this also your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly see page 4 in the B/C/S and page 4 in English. We should focus on paragraph 21, and what we need is on page 5 in English. I just wanted to show the paragraph begins on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told me, Mr. Radan, that the name of the hotel on this page is wrong. It says "Central Hotel." What should be the name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Hotel Bristol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So after this correction, does this statement faithfully reflect what you've told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: What's missing is an elevation from which there was sniper fire against the population at Vrace and Grbavica almost on a daily basis. So from three sides we were shelled and sniped at every day, and we had just a narrow exit from Grbavica and Vrace towards Lukavica and Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where would this correction be, in which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: It would be in paragraph 21, because it deals with sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After these corrections, does your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness said that an elevation is missing. Does that elevation have a name? Then we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. He told us the name, that it is probably missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the name of this elevation from which the sniper fired?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Asimovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was not on the transcript, if I -- yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I can assist, I would spell the name. It's almost correct, but it's -- the name of the hill is A-s-i-m-o-v-o.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have all the details. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So after these corrections, Mr. Radan, does your written statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: With these additions, everything remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender Mr. Radan's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1608 receives number D466, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would have few more questions for this witness, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but before that I would read the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A short summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope it will fit into 32 lines, or 35 lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's three lines extra. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To speed up a bit, I'll read in English. Branko Radan was born in Topljik, Novo Sarajevo municipality. After the multi-party elections, he noticed the boundaries between the people of the three nationalities become thicker and deeper. There were already talks about the arming of Muslims and the formation of units of the Green Berets and Patriotic League. He saw groups of young men wearing green berets walking around town, and shots fired from infantry weapons were heard in the evening. Unlike the Muslims and Croats, the Serbs were not arming and preparing for war. At the start of the war, Mr. Radan, Branko, was president of the executive authority, Executive Board of Novo Sarajevo municipality. Municipality authorities took the stand that were -- that there must not be any discrimination, and, in particular, no torture or abuse of the non-Serbian population and security should be guaranteed to all. There was a group of nine Serb -- Serbian men who created major problems for Muslims and Croats in the area. The executive authority, following several meetings, requested and demanded that the nine men be removed from the Grbavica area by local police organs. Eventually they were removed. Whatever humanitarian aid arrived in the municipality, it was distributed equally among the different ethnicities in the municipality. Grbavica was shelled from the Muslim side with increasing frequency, but most victims were killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side. For protection against that, the inhabitants of Grbavica used to erect blinds several metres tall. Due to difficult material situation of the people, the executive authority made use of the humanitarian aid to organise people's kitchen, public kitchen, where the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats households obtained food without any problem. That would be the summary, but I would pose a few additional questions to this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radan, could you please take a look at paragraph 19 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what we need on the screen is 65 ter 1D1608.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So paragraph 19, this is what you say there: You say that all Croats and Muslims who were in the territory of Novo Sarajevo received pensions and humanitarian aid from the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in relation to this paragraph, let us take a look at 1D2120. This is a press release by SRNA. Could we please focus on the second paragraph. We need the second sentence. In B/C/S, it starts with "otklanjaju," and in English with the words, "all the difficulties". So we see here that a press release was issued. It is the 22nd of July, 1992. And it says in this document: "All the difficulties that the citizens had are being effectively dealt with, regardless of their nationality."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you have the opportunity of seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. A copy was provided to me as well. May I give my comment with regard to paragraph 19 and also may I say something about the press release of SRNA? We, in Grbavica and in Vrace, in this urban part of Novo Sarajevo, we took a certain position. At that moment, there were 2.000 Muslims, and perhaps 300 or 400 Croats. At the very outset, we collected all the certificates stating who had been entitled to a pension before the war. Such persons automatically became entitled to receive a pension, not only Serbs but also Croats and Muslims. That was a way of avoiding discrimination against these persons who stayed with us. Because if we think that if we took the right attitude when we made every effort to remain in Yugoslavia, a common state, when all of that failed, then we decided to defend what we believed was ours and in our territory. If these people remained in our territory, then, in my view, they gave more legality and legitimacy to us by virtue of the fact that they stayed on, so they were entitled to social insurance, to the food that was organised in soup kitchens and so on, so they were in the same position as the Serbs were. This letter that was given by Mr. Sipcic to SRNA confirms that our position was correct and that the way we treated our fellow citizens was proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned this, I think, but maybe it wasn't clear. I just want to ask you whether Muslims and Croats also received medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. At the health centre in Grbavica they enjoyed the same rights. After all, at the medical centre in Grbavica, we had an excellent lady doctor, an ethnic Muslim, Dr. Mirsada. She was a pediatrician. She stayed there throughout the war. Attempts were made to remove her from there but I said very explicitly: Only when you bring a Serb who is a better doctor, then we are going to find a new job for Mrs. Mirsada. To this day she comes to Lukavica and our Serb children go to her, to Grbavica, so that she can treat them. This is exceptional confidence that was instilled in people while she worked there in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, most part of the answer is already in the statement, so there's no need, Mr. Radan, to repeat what we found already in your statement, such as the story of Dr. Mirsada. Have you dealt with the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. I would just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- one additional question. The -- this press -- what seems to be a kind of a press release, but it also reads: "The number of citizens returning the illegally obtained property to the authorities is higher and higher." Who obtained illegally property? Because it's -- it's totally unclear to me what is referred to here. Could you explain why, when, by whom, property was illegally obtained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Individuals who thought that the war would be over very quickly and what they obtained in an unfair way would remain theirs. However, the police and the military police took action with the assistance of the civilian authorities or, rather, on the recommendation of the civilian authorities. It was stated over our radio that this property should be returned, and that those who intend to return that should return that to the military police and that it should be recorded accordingly. Certain individuals did return these stolen goods, that would be the right word, that did not belong to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And individuals. What do I have to think about? Were these housewives who went around stealing property of others? Or what -- what is the reference to these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly the male population, military conscripts or civilians who did not have military obligation. Also there were housewives that had no other way of getting supplies and that is how they obtained supplies or, rather, that is how they met their needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was there any division as far as ethnicity is concerned? Was it Croats rather than Muslims, or Serbs rather than Croats? Who -- who illegally obtained property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be insincere if I were to say that the Serbs were not the most numerous. So the Serbs were certainly the most numerous in terms of the commission of these unlawful activities on the ground. Croats and Muslims, I think, were fearful in this situation, which is only natural, and I don't think that they were not so inclined to take such action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And property was taken from other Serbs or from Croats or Muslims or equally divided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for the most part, the others. Serbs from non-Serbs. That was the objective. So if people would find out at a given point in time that the owner of an apartment was not there, then that was dealt with very quickly. Or, rather, things were prevented by way of military action, military police, civilian police, so attempts were made to stop such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that clarifies, to some extent, this document. This was presented by you, Mr. Lukic, in relation to paragraph 19 of the statement. Could you have a look at paragraph 19 of the statement because, irrespective of your questions, could you read it again, Mr. Radan. The paragraph states, and you repeated that a minute ago, that -- and why Croats and Muslims in Novo Sarajevo received their pensions and humanitarian aid. And then it continues by saying: "As part of that, an exchange was organised when 15 to 20 buses with Serbs left Sarajevo, and this was on the Vrbanja bridge." I have difficulties in linking the provision of pensions and humanitarian aids to Croats and Muslims with an exchange where 15 to 20 buses with Serbs left Sarajevo. I -- I didn't understand the relation between the two matters mentioned here. Could you explain how this -- the one would be a part of the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try. There's a mention of 15 to 20 buses here. This is mentioned by way of affirming the good will that existed. That is to say, Serbs, in their territory, showed good will. They did not carry out an aggression against the Croats and Muslims. They enjoyed the same rights. There is the reference to 15 or 20 buses here. They did not leave. Well, they did not leave then. They did not leave Sarajevo then but only on the 15th of November, 1992. That was afterwards. May I explain this completely? Well, then I'd have to go into a completely different paragraph. That has to do the 30th of September. The Muslims going from Grbavica to Sarajevo. So all of that is interlinked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because if you talk about an exchange, then, of course, I would like to know what was exchanged against what. The paragraph is unclear on that. Perhaps, Mr. Lukic, if at any later point, or Ms. Bibles, could seek clarification of what exactly the link between the two events is, which, as I now understand, was at a later stage. What was exchanged and how the one is an expression of the good will which is expressed by the pensions as well. I leave it to the parties at this moment to further clarify, but it's unclear to me. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're on the subject, Mr. Radan, could you please explain to us and the Court so that we don't have to go back to that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Now why am I saying that this is linked to the 30th? First of all, it wasn't an exchange. There was no exchange. These crossings-over did not have to do with an exchange. What happened on 30th of October, 1992, when the Muslims crossed the Vrbanja bridge in the morning at 0615, that was agreement reached on the spot between the Serb and Muslim side. There was this internal agreement reached, that is to say, neighbours agreed at the front line, the Jewish cemetery, Gornji Kovacici, Donji Kovacici, Vrbanja bridge, they could not take the fire that was there every day. Serbs removed part of their families to other houses where their friends and relatives lived. The Muslims had nowhere else to go so on the 30th of September, in the morning at 0615, the Muslims crossed the Vrbanja bridge. That had been agreed upon. So in that way, some signal was given to the other side in Sarajevo too. And then it shows that immediately that morning, at 0620, on the east river, this piece of news was carried. So why am I linking this, why am I saying that this is a goodwill gesture? On the 15th of November, that is to say, a month and a half later, 20 buses of Serbs left Sarajevo through Lukavica and went to Pale, Serbia, and so on. That is to say, without any problem whatsoever. They left the other side and came to our territory. But it was not an exchange. It was simply a gesture of good will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the latter part of your answer, it was a gesture of good will that you received those Serbs which were leaving the Presidency-controlled side and went to Pale. Is -- or -- because I see your point, that you say: We allowed Muslims to leave at 0615 in the morning over the Vrbanja bridge. I see that -- that apparently you interpret this as meeting their wishes, if I understand you well. Now, how do I have to understand the 20 buses of Serbs as an expression of your good intentions? Is that by receiving them or by -- it's a bit unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a response to our good will, the good will of the Serb side. That is to say, this statement that we, the authorities, allowed them to cross over on the 30th of September. That's not right. Because we did not take part in these discussions. The authorities did not take part in that at all. This was an internal agreement reached on the spot. Neighbours agreed to do such and such a thing. Now, this was done well. There was no reaction on the other side. No one said that there was expulsion or this or that. Then our response to this good will, the fact that we allowed people -- or, rather, that they agreed of their own free will to cross over to the other side and then they allowed those buses full of Serbs to leave Sarajevo, so we did not receive anyone. This is just a gesture. That is where their hold was no longer so firm, that of their government, that they would not allow anyone to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there was good will on both sides, letting those leave and this was not organised by the authorities but was, rather, organised by the people themselves, if I understand you well. And the first gesture was from the Serb side and then later, from the other side, a similar gesture was made. Mr. Lukic, to say that this was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you said. I interrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these two cases, yes, good will was expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to say that this story becomes immediately clear from reading paragraph 19, I would say it doesn't. Statements should provide us with information which assists us in understanding what the witness's testimony is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just offer this document for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2120 receives number D467, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask a question with respect to this paragraph 19. Sir, what year are we talking about when this Serbian authorities gave Muslims and Croats pensions and humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immediately at the beginning of 1992. It was in July, when we collected proof and evidence of the right to pension. It was in July of 1992. From then on, they kept on receiving their retirement dues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So as early as July 1992, this area was already being controlled by Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Had it always been like that before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, earlier we were not divided and there were no divisions by where people lived. But we're talking about a majority, a majority Serbian population lived there. Most of the people were Serbs but previously nobody paid attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking about the authorities. When did the authorities become exclusively Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exclusively Serb, in 1992, when we were no longer allowed to use our Assembly building and all of its resources. Lines had been drawn, and the municipality building and the church were on the other side of the Miljacka river which means we had to establish a new government, authorities, infrastructure, everything that was needed to enable the functioning of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a short follow-up question in that respect. Sir, you said: "From July 1992 on, they," the Croats and Muslims, "kept on receiving their retirement dues. " How long did that -- or up to which moment was that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They kept receiving their pension money for as long as they stayed in our territory. For as long as they were in our territory until reintegration. And then when the territory was reintegrated, they continued claiming their rights wherever they decided to stay and reside. And the reintegration was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Those who stayed there received the pensions throughout the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So I think I offered this document into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just check. And I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You offered it and it's D467. And then page 35, line 8, I said: "And is admitted into evidence."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radan, I'm taking over from the Presiding Judge and the other Judges. Did any of the convoys with humanitarian aid for the Muslim territory, i.e., the territory under the control of the BiH Army, pass through your territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. From the beginning of the war, from May 1992, roads were not good. Tvrnici [phoen] was on a macadam road. The convoys did pass through that territory. At Lukavica we would be waiting for them. We would check what was being sent. We talked to them. We tried to ascertain what was in the convoys. We're talking about various humanitarian and charity organisations that collected aid and sent it to the population in Sarajevo. I remember well that in May 1992 the current cardinal, Vinko Puljic was a member of one of the teams. We received him. We gave him a cup of coffee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please slow down so that the interpreters are able to translate for us, to interpret for us, what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise the name was not recorded. Who was a member of the delegation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Vinko Puljic, who is currently the cardinal in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it was not only that humanitarian aid but the other aid also came. And together with the military representative of UNPROFOR, Mr. Zarkovic reorganised things and we tried to let the convoys go, but the Muslim side was not always co-operative and they didn't allow the same thing to happen. So, on several occasions, we had to unload the goods because it was not received in Sarajevo for reasons known only to them. A lot of the goods perished in Lukavica and at other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 13 of your statement, which I would like to call up, it is 1D1608. In this paragraph, you talk about the group of nine Serbs who created problems in Grbavica. I suppose that we could call them criminals. Did those criminals cause problems for the Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: It would be my personal view if I said that they created problems for me as well, but it's not neither here nor there. They did create problems for the Serbs. If they were not satisfied with what they could get from the other two ethnic groups, i.e., Muslims and Croats, they did not refrain, and usually that happened when they were drunk, and then they did not make a distinction and they did things that normal people wouldn't do. In front of the municipality building, they shot at my car because they were drunk and I lost my car, but it is really not important. The most important thing would have been the image that we wanted to create of ourselves and the way we wanted to be perceived by the other two ethnic groups, i.e., Muslims and Croats. We wanted to be perceived as peaceful people, we wanted to protect those people, and that's why we suggested that those nine people, in co-ordination with the civilian and military police and the civilian authorities, that those people should be removed from our territory because we didn't want them to go on creating problems for us. Gradually that was done, all of them were removed from the territory, and two -- and two years later, they were no longer in our territories. In other words, they stayed in our territory, no longer than two or three years at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again invite the witness to -- to reduce your speed of speech. And you said "two or three years." Do you know exactly or at least in what month they were removed? I mean, three years from 1992 brings us into 1995. When -- could you tell us approximately what month were they effectively removed? What year, what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The protagonists, the ones who created the most problems -- or, rather, the main protagonist, Batko, was removed in September or October 1992 from our territory. He would go away and then come back and then go away and finally he was removed. And then the others, I know only their nicknames, when the ring leader left the territory, they were no longer such a big problem and they could easily be and gradually removed from the territory. They were mostly locals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm mainly interested in the time when none of them was left, when they effectively were removed. And you're confusing me a bit by referring to Batko, saying, "he was away and then come back and then go away and then finally he was removed." When was that finally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am testifying about the period when I was the president of the Executive Board, and that was up to March 1993. This would cover the period of which I have relevant knowledge. The first time they left the territory was in September or October 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be clear that I'm mainly interested in when they last left the territory. Because if they return meanwhile, that may not resolve the problem entirely. So when did they last leave the territory, without then returning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, and I say that my knowledge spans a period up to March 1993, and the biggest problem was eliminated when Batko left. The others were also problematic. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm asking you when -- and if you want to make a distinction, Batko left for the last time and never returned on that moment, that's fine, and for the others, give me another time-frame. But that's what I would like to know: When did Batko leave and did not return any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that he left in September/October. That was the first time he left our territory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think my question was clear enough. I didn't ask you when he for the first time left. I'm asking when he definitely left. That is, the last time he left and did not return. So to repeat all the other answers is not of great assistance to me. If you don't know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is very clear and my answer was very clear. I told you that my knowledge spans a period up to March 1992 and -- and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether you fortunately succeeded in removing them is, in the end, as far as time is concerned, is rather unclear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the executive branch of power provides suggestions and tries to co-operate with the civilian and military police and -- and the military, in order to see how the territory could be made safer, by removing such elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your good intentions and the efforts you made. I'm talking about the result described in your statement as that, fortunately, they were successful in removing these men from Grbavica. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking about these men, these criminals, were they independent or were they a part of a system, either a military or a civilian system?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: They were not a part of the system. They just wore units -- uniforms, but they were not members of any unit. They were not recorded. Nobody knew from which position they acted. In other words, they were not a part of any system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who succeeded you in your position as the president of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Mr. Budo Obradovic, the late Budo Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I seek clarification with respect to the uniforms. Can you describe which kind of uniforms they wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At first, those uniforms were of all kinds. People wore what they could. And then there was an official declaration as to how a soldier should look like what he should wear in order to be recognised as a soldier. At first, it was really very random.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to interrupt you. I was referring to your last answer with respect to the nine men. You said: "They wore uniforms ..." What kind of uniforms, these nine men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually they wore the best uniform, but they were not soldiers. They wore the best uniforms. I don't know how they had obtained them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking you what kind of uniforms they had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Camouflage uniforms. Camouflage uniforms. Camouflage uniforms. They looked like military uniforms, and they obtained them in various ways. I'm talking about camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which -- which colour and which kind of insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, they did not sport any insignia. It depended on what they needed to achieve. They could change those insignia at will. They did not have their own identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you ever seen these men personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What colour did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've told you, they had camouflage greenish-brownish uniforms, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was exactly my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just intervene and it can be checked probably in audio recording. Page 42, line 16. It was recorded that the witness said: "They looked like military uniforms." The witness said: "They looked close to military uniforms." And I will check [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's -- yes, you can verify that and if you could reach an agreement at least that there is a slight difference between "like" and "close." It is both similarity but the one stronger than the other, that's clear. Please proceed. Any further questions, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but I think it's the break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the break time. But before we break, how much time would you need after the break. We had an early break last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably less than five minutes, couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would suggest that we take those initial -- those other five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. We'll try not to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, I'm coming to the end of my examination. You were succeeded by the late Budimir Obradovic, as you've told us. What happened to him? And why? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Budimir Obradovic joined from the military. He tried to implement the same military discipline. He met with resistance from those who were not very keen on implementing the law. Very soon thereafter, he was found dead, he was killed in his office, because he didn't meet the requests of those who had wanted him to help them do something against the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I would finish with paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to see the following page on the screen, and I'm talking about the same statement that is already in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What remains unclear here is when you talk about the shelling in -- near the students' residences -- residential buildings and then along Moravska Street, populated mostly by the Pandurevic and Cecar families. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: They were Serbs. Do you need any further explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did the fire come from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: We saw it and the observers also saw it and made it clear that the shells came from Velesici. They were fired from a mobile mortar which was on rail tracks, so one could not establish the exact location where they were. Shells fell near the halls of residence and along Moravska Street from Velesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, that was all we had for you. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take the break now. Mr. Radan, we'll take a break for 20 minutes. We'll resume at five minutes past 12.00. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at five minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, I have to inform the parties that Judge Fluegge is unable to continue hearing this case but only for one session due to urgent Tribunal matters. Judge Moloto and myself, we have considered whether it would be in the interests of justice to continue to hear the case at this moment, and we decided it is. Therefore, we'll sit 15 bis for this session, most likely, only. Ms. Bibles, the estimate was two hours for this witness for cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe that's an accurate estimate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I also do understand that the next Defence witness would be available only tomorrow morning. Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were thinking and consulting whether to bring him, and then when we realized it was likely to be at 2.00, we thought we'd better not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be a sensible solution for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Bibles. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, your statement identifies that you had a role in municipal organs of Novo Sarajevo, but the relevant dates for that service is not provided in your statement. Because that timing can make a difference to the basis of your knowledge, I'd like to start by going through some of those dates. First, was your first involvement in local government in December 1991 when you became a member of the local municipal or commune board of Vrace?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: It was not government. It was involvement only in the party in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So this was an SDS board that you became part of in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, prior to December of 1991, were you active in the work of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Prior to December of 1991, would you agree that your source of information was publicly available, such as the media, public speeches, Assembly sessions, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, all the sources were public, but what I accept and acknowledge is my personal choice. But everybody had a free choice of whatever they wanted to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, once you were on the SDS board, did you begin to have access to more information about events on the ground in Vrace?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, but only within our local commune where I was actively involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. And you'd agree that sometimes you would relay that information in your local area up the chain of SDS hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I did not have such a role as to spread information. I was only a member of the local board of the SDS at Vrace, without any specific tasks or mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: But you had some ability to contact the republican-level Bosnian Serb leadership even in that position. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. We had some access, although it was not completely free. You couldn't go there for talks whenever you wished. But through local boards at municipal level, we could make certain initiatives and make inquiries into matters that were of interest to ask -- to us, so we would contact the Municipal Board and they would then contact higher levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, in fact, in February 1992, working with the other local SDS boards in Novo Sarajevo, you requested the presidents of the Bosnian Serb leadership and Radovan Karadzic himself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: He was asked -- Radovan Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership were asked to come to the local SDS meeting to assist in resolving some internal issues or some political issues; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: The issue was agreeing on how to preside over the Municipal Board of the SDS.
